section_name: What Is a Mini-Lesson — Definition and Characteristics
content:
Episode 2: Planning and Delivering Writing Mini-Lessons (K-12)

I want to dive more deeply into the INSTRUCTION piece... specifically the PLANNING and DELIVERY of whole-class MINI lessons.

We often use the term "lesson" to represent time spent teaching any concept or topic. Consequently, to distinguish a writing lesson from other learning experiences... it's called a MINI LESSON. A mini lesson IS a type of lesson... although it's shorter, punchier... and emphasizes HOW to do something in writing.

Mini-lessons are:
- Tier 1 instruction, as they are delivered to the whole class, ensuring everyone has access to grade-level writing knowledge.
- Mini-lessons are Standards-based. They focus on the specific skills outlined within your Language Arts writing standards.
- Mini-lessons are MINI in that they are ONLY 10-15 minutes long.
- They are NARROWly focused on a Single skill.
- And... mini-lessons are Strategic. They don't just explain WHAT a skill is but detail HOW to do it in writing.

Episode 2: Planning and Delivering Writing Mini-Lessons (K-12)

Every 15-minute writing mini-lesson moves through 4 steps. Now, these aren't MY steps. I didn't make them up. These are part of best practice, direct instruction. Each purposeful step is supported by educational research... and is defined as a component of high-quality instruction.

Throughout this episode, I will describe EACH of the four steps. And while I do, I encourage you to reflect on your own current practices.
- Identify the elements of your writing lessons that are inline with these best practices... and commit to KEEPING them.
- Simultaneously, consider what you may need to START doing within your writing mini-lessons...
- And even things you may need to TWEAK or STOP.

Then... at the end of this video, I'll help you to use those discoveries to determine your NEXT STEPS in planning and delivering dynamic writing instruction.

Episode 2: Planning and Delivering Writing Mini-Lessons (K-12) — Step 1: Introduce the Skill

Every mini-lesson begins with the introduction of the skill, ingredient, or technique being taught. For example...

"Writers, we've been learning how to write persuasively. We are getting better at stating a reason and supporting it with evidence. Now today, I want to teach you how to flow smoothly from one reason to the next, from one body paragraph to the next. SO... today's mini-lesson is on choosing the right transition.. and knowing how to do this will improve the trait of organization."

OR, maybe you're a kindergarten or EL teacher and delivering a mini-lesson on labeling. It may start like this..

"Hey writers, you are doing a great job of including lots of accurate and close-up details within your pictorial writing. TODAY I want to teach you how you can tell your reader even MORE information by adding letter labels to your pictures. When we learn to do this our trait of ideas is getting better."

Step 1 should take 30 seconds — or less. Remember, a mini-lesson is focused on HOW to do something... ONE THING... in writing.

section_name: Step 1: What Skills to Teach and Purpose of the Introduction
content:
Episode 2: Planning and Delivering Writing Mini-Lessons (K-12) — Step 1: What Skills to Teach

Now, let me pause for a moment and anticipate some may be wondering: What are the skills I'm supposed to teach in these writing mini-lessons? And to answer that question, I'm going to reference the hyperlink on your note-taking handout. Within the digital handout, you can click on that icon to access a list of the MINI skills that are to be delivered in mini LESSONS... These are the very skills outlined within the K-12 standards for persuasive, informative, and narrative writing.

So the purpose of Step 1 is to ANNOUNCE the SKILL that you are going to teach.
- It's a declarative couple of sentences. It's not a question.
- We aren't starting up a discussion.
- And we aren't introducing today's writing TOPIC.

Step 1 identifies A SINGLE... grade-level writing SKILL... and it should take 30 seconds to introduce.

section_name: Step 2: Instruct on the Skill — Overview and Step 2A (Tell)
content:
Episode 2: Planning and Delivering Writing Mini-Lessons (K-12) — Step 2: Instruct on the Skill

Step 2 is the core of instruction. It's the meatiest, most important, AND longest step of a mini-lesson. Step 2 is presented in two parts — Tell THEN Show.

Step 2A is approximately 5 minutes long... and is when you TELL students ABOUT the skill. This is when the teacher clearly explains WHAT the skill is, WHY writers use it, WHEN and WHERE to apply it, and HOW it functions within writing. Step 2A establishes foundational knowledge OF the skill.

But, as many experienced teachers know... just because a student can define WHAT a topic sentence is doesn't mean he knows HOW to WRITE one to organize his own details. A student may know OF transitions but doesn't know HOW to choose the appropriate one for the point she is making. Kindergartners may know WHAT a picture label looks like but not HOW to incorporate one into their own pictorial writings.

section_name: Step 2B: Show — Modeling with Think Aloud
content:
Episode 2: Planning and Delivering Writing Mini-Lessons (K-12) — Step 2B: Show

THIS is the purpose of Step 2B — to SHOW students HOW to execute the skill that you just told them about. In other words... in Step 2B you will DO the skill... LIVE... and in front of the students.

- For example, in a lesson on transitions, Step 2B would include me demonstrating HOW to insert a transition connecting a couple of previously-written sentences...
- OR in kindergarten, Step 2B would include me demonstrating HOW to add letter labels to a pre-drawn picture or photograph.

During the 5 minutes of Step 2B the teacher has a dual responsibility. WHILE executing an example, she should reveal the journey of her thinking. Teaching writing includes teaching THINKING, which is why modeling an EXAMPLE is to be paired with an ORAL Think Aloud.

Writing is a complex process. It's not just about the final product; it's about the journey to get there. So, we need to show students how our thinking progresses as we execute this new writing skill. For example, my Think Aloud when demonstrating how to insert a transition within a paragraph may include thoughts about...
- determining WHERE I need a transition...
- WHICH TYPE of transition is appropriate
- and how to CHOOSE the one that fits best.

section_name: Step 2B: The Power of the Think Aloud
content:
Episode 2: Planning and Delivering Writing Mini-Lessons (K-12) — Step 2B: The Power of the Think Aloud

This slow-motion thinking process is what students need to hear. Most kids know WHAT a transition is... and even WHY it's necessary. But without an EXPLICIT think aloud from their teacher, most students will continue to just PICK a transition from a list of options we gave them.. and kerplunk it into their writing.... where it doesn't even fit.

When we accompany a visual example with the invisible think aloud, students get a peek INSIDE a writer's brain. They hear how we start the skill... encounter challenges... and how we overcome them.

Think Alouds build STRATEGIC writers who can problem-solve and persevere. Your thoughts DURING the mini-lesson... become the students' thoughts AFTER the mini-lesson. When they attempt the skill, your modeling AND thinking are what they rely on. They start to hear YOUR voice, YOUR thoughts in THEIR writers' brains. And that's our ultimate goal... to teach ourselves out of a job. These kids don't need us anymore!

Back in kindergarten, adding a Think Aloud WHILE labeling a picture makes the skill even more EXPLICIT to 5 year olds. It would include sharing thoughts about...
- HOW do I figure out a picture detail that NEEDS a label?
- WHERE do I put the label on the paper?
- HOW do I determine which letters to write down?

section_name: Step 2B: The I Do — Transition, Pronouns, and Direct Instruction
content:
Episode 2: Planning and Delivering Writing Mini-Lessons (K-12) — Step 2B: The I Do

When transitioning FROM the 5 minutes of telling TO the 5 minutes of showing, many teachers do so by simply saying... "Let me show you how a writer would do this." Note the pronouns.... Let ME... show YOU. Again, Step 2B is the I DO. It's where the teacher does ALL of the thinking, ALL of the talking, and ALL of the writing. This IS direct instruction... students learn DIRECTLY from the teacher.

Step 2B is about DOING an example... WHILE talking through the steps, decisions, challenges, and choices you make as a writer. Although the goal is for students to be able to execute the skill independently and successfully... it starts with the teacher modeling first. This occurs in Step 2B. It's the I DO. This is the first phase of the Gradual Release of Responsibility.
- After the I DO, then WE will work together, sharing the responsibility, in order to apply the skill in a second example.
- We WILL end the lesson outlining the YOU DO task, where students will continue to practice the skill.

BEFORE the release, though, teachers have to do an example while sharing their thoughts... and this is relevant at ALL grade levels.

section_name: Step 2B: Why the Teacher Does the First Example Alone
content:
Episode 2: Planning and Delivering Writing Mini-Lessons (K-12) — Step 2B: Why the Teacher Does the First Example Alone

Remember a MINI lesson isn't like other learning experiences that we provide. There ARE times to begin new learning with inquiry-based strategies.. but that's not how you begin a writing mini-lesson. There are times to engage students in classroom discussions... but not during the writing mini-lesson. This 15 minutes is focused on providing direct, explicit instruction on a specific grade-level writing skill. Consequently, the I DO in Step 2B is a one-sided conversation. It's a monologue, not a dialogue.
- The teacher doesn't ask the students questions. He tells the students information.
- He doesn't ask the kids to help... he does it all on his own.

In fact, by its name, the I DO implies that ONLY I, the teacher, am doing the work right now. YOU, the students, are to watch and listen to me.

Now, I recognize that what I'm describing maybe a major paradigm shift... But let me point out a couple things about DOING the first example all by ourselves... When we involve students in the "I Do," we tend to call on the same high-performing students... because they are the ones with their hands up! But the "Think Aloud" is designed for students who are struggling to grasp the skill. Even with a peer giving the answer, many students are left wondering HOW they got the answer... WHAT steps did they take? And HOW did they know to do that? THESE are the thought processes that teacher-only think alouds provide.

Therefore, make sure students know that during a writing mini-lesson, you will do the first example all by yourself... and they shouldn't help you.

section_name: Step 2B: Student Engagement During the I Do
content:
Episode 2: Planning and Delivering Writing Mini-Lessons (K-12) — Step 2B: Student Engagement During the I Do

A SECOND point I want to make is that we can still engage students during an I DO — even if they aren't talking. There's a common misconception that student engagement is solely measured by active participation. While students raising their hands and offering input IS a sign they are engaged, it's not the only indicator. We can also gauge student involvement by observing their behaviors.... Like watching to see if they are leaning in and listening actively to the think aloud, following the teacher with their eyes as she moves, or showing nonverbal cues of understanding like the subtle nodding of their heads.

section_name: Step 3: Interaction — The WE DO with Turn and Talk
content:
Episode 2: Planning and Delivering Writing Mini-Lessons (K-12) — Step 3: Interaction

When preparing to teach a writing MINI lesson, you INTRODUCE the skill in 30 seconds or less... You then provide direct instruction by TELLING about and SHOWING how to execute it. This then leads us to STEP 3... and the WE DO.

Step 3 empowers students to attempt the skill. However... Many teachers reveal a second example and ask... What transition would you use here? Or... What label would you write? This isn't very gradual. In fact, only those who fully understand the skill and how it works can raise their hands and answer the question... and that usually includes only a couple students... and often the same ones who were TRYING to help you in the I DO.

The purpose of Step 3.. and the WE DO... is to guide ALL students through the SAME small steps and decision-making that you modeled previously.

It's important to note that the teacher is still VERY INVOLVED in the WE DO and the execution of the skill. The students are only HELPING with this next example... In fact, that's how most teachers MOVE from Step 2 to Step 3... they say... "Help me with the next one."

Step 3 is intended to get every student to attempt the skill... ORALLY.. via a turn and talk.
skill_title: The WE DO with Turn and Talk

section_name: Step 3: Turn and Talk Example — Transitions Mini-Lesson
content:
Episode 2: Planning and Delivering Writing Mini-Lessons (K-12) — Step 3: Turn and Talk Example

Let me describe how Step 3 might look in the transitions mini-lesson.

The teacher presents a second pair of sentences and says... "Class, the writer has to determine WHERE a transition would be helpful. Where are you thinking it should go? Turn and talk." After a few moments, I say "Back to me.... I heard many of you tell your partner that you would insert a transition here."... pointing at the sentence set.

Then I would remind students that we have a list of MANY transitions, but I need to narrow down the TYPE of transition that fits with the TYPE of information stated in the sentences. So I might reread the first sentence... and then the second sentence... and ask about how the details are related.... "What TYPE or category of transition do you need here? Turn and talk." Again, after a few moments, I say "Back to me" and announce what I overheard. "Many of you said it's a contrasting detail... so it needs a contrasting transition."

The final step of MY Think Aloud was choosing WHICH of the transitions in the category worked best. So, I need to pose that same question to the children. After rereading the different options aloud, I might say, "So all of these COULD work. They are all contrasting transitions. BUT which would you choose? Which one sounds the best — and why? Turn and talk." Moments later, I say "Back to me" and identify the transition word(s) that would be appropriate.

section_name: Step 3: The WE DO Process — Turn and Talk Mechanics
content:
Episode 2: Planning and Delivering Writing Mini-Lessons (K-12) — Step 3: WE DO Process and Turn and Talk Mechanics

Step 3 and the WE DO guides students through the same process they observed the teacher execute in the I DO. This time, though, the teacher tees-up the thinking... poses the question, pauses.. and encourages the STUDENTS to think through the answer WITH A PEER. This encourages ALL students to think like a writer — not just the ones with their hands raised.

A turn-and-talk is a brief, focused response to a question the teacher poses. When the teacher says "Turn and talk"... students quickly face a designated partner to share their thoughts.
- This lasts for about 10 seconds... that's it.
- Remember, it's not a discussion.. it's a few moments to think of a specific answer to a focused question.

When students turn and talk, the teacher eavesdrops and reads lips... Based on what she's seeing and hearing, she knows who is and isn't starting to get it. After turn-and-talk time, the teacher announces "Back to me." The TEACHER reveals what she saw and heard DURING the turn and talk.... RATHER than calling on any single student. The teacher summarizes and validates the correct answers she heard. OR... if most students struggled during the turn and talk.... then the teacher REVEALS the correct response... followed with a review or clarification of the skill.

Remember, how we started Step 3... "Help me with the next one" meaning... I'm doing ANOTHER ONE... YOU help me. Helping implies, the students are doing what they can... but the teacher is right there to do the work that they can't... and then reteaching as needed.

By NOT calling on students and NOT bringing individuals to the board, you will be able to maintain control of your ticking time. Remember, Step 3 is about 5 minutes. You have ONLY about 5 minutes to guide them through the ENTIRE second example.

section_name: Step 4: Closure — Recap and Release the YOU DO
content:
Episode 2: Planning and Delivering Writing Mini-Lessons (K-12) — Step 4: Closure

Step 4 — concludes the lesson and provides 2 pieces of information... the RECAP and the RESPONSE.

Begin with a quick RECAP of the skill... "Today I was teaching you how to choose the right transition to connect your sentences"... OR... "Today's lesson was all about adding MORE information for your reader by adding labels to your picture."

Then identify the YOU DO task. This is the RESPONSE. This YOU DO won't happen IN the lesson. It happens AFTER the lesson. In Step 4, we are simply describing what students will do during the writing time that follows this mini-lesson.

Since we have modeled the skill TWICE — I do and We do — it shouldn't take more than 30 seconds to tell the topic they are working with. The YOU DO should be a parallel experience to the examples used in the lesson.

- If all the teacher did was read 2 sentences, determine where to put a transition, the type needed, and which one works best... then that's what the students do.. using SEVERAL different sentence sets.. and maybe some from their own previous writings.
- If the teacher taught us to add labels to a previous drawing, then that's what the YOU DO is. Return to a previous drawing, and add labels applying the same process learned in the mini-lesson.
skill_title: Recap and Release the YOU DO

section_name: Summary — Key Takeaways for Planning and Delivering Mini-Lessons
content:
Episode 2: Planning and Delivering Writing Mini-Lessons (K-12) — Summary

As I wrap up this video, let me identify the most important takeaways. TEACHING WRITING requires that we plan and deliver mini-lessons that...
- Introduce a grade-level skill.
- Tell what it is and tell how it works.
- Model the skill while thinking aloud.
- Model again with students' help.
- Provide a parallel task for students to do after the mini-lesson.

Whether you teach students who write with pencils, crayons, or keyboards... this is how to teach grade-level standards-based writing skills.

I encourage you to:
- Identify the elements of EACH step that you are executing effectively...
- And determine a couple areas that you could polish and refine.

By consistently delivering effective mini-lessons, we take the next step toward building better writers.
skill_title: Key Takeaways for Planning and Delivering Mini-Lessons
